passage:
The sentence I hear most from my aunt Tanuja is "You don't know the world yet." I'm Sabina, twenty-five, and I have a job, a lease and a savings account. Last Diwali I mentioned my idea about changing teams at work, and she said it again, patting my hand.
It stung. For a moment I wanted to snap. But I love her, so I breathed and said, "Aunty, you know a lot I don't. May I explain my idea fully first? Then tell me where I'm missing something. I'd really like that."
She was quiet, then said, "Okay. Say it." She listened for ten minutes and asked two questions. It was the first time.

qa.q: What sentence does Sabina hear most from aunt Tanuja?
qa.a: Sabina hears, "You don't know the world yet."

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when Tanuja said the sentence at Diwali?
qa.a: Sabina felt hurt and tempted to snap. Choosing to breathe and speak calmly shows that love for Tanuja won over the sting.

qa.q: What did Sabina say that shifted the pattern?
qa.a: Sabina acknowledged that Tanuja knows much, asked to explain the idea fully first, and invited Tanuja to point out what was missing. It asked for a real hearing without a fight.

qa.q: What might Tanuja have been feeling when going quiet before saying "Okay. Say it."?
qa.a: Tanuja may have felt surprised and perhaps a little humbled, since Sabina had invited her to add wisdom. Listening for ten minutes and asking two questions shows real attention.

grounding: A young adult is told "you don't know the world yet" and calmly asks the elder aunt for a real hearing.

passage:
Jasleen's uncle Harbhajan arrived late for Sunday lunch and I, Keerthana, Jasleen's friend, sat opposite. Every time Jasleen spoke, the uncle waved a hand: "You don't know the world yet, puttar."
The third time, Jasleen's fork stopped. I saw a jaw tighten. I don't know if it was anger or hurt.
Then, quiet and steady, Jasleen said, "Uncle-ji, I probably don't know everything. But could you give me two minutes without interrupting? Then tell me what I've missed."
Nobody moved. Harbhajan blinked, then sat back. "Two minutes. Go."
Jasleen spoke. The uncle asked one question at the end, and it wasn't dismissive.

qa.q: How many minutes did Jasleen ask for?
qa.a: Jasleen asked for two minutes without interrupting.

qa.q: What might Jasleen have been feeling when the fork stopped and the jaw tightened?
qa.a: Jasleen may have felt hurt or angry, though Keerthana says the cause is not certain. The stopped fork and tight jaw show something was building.

qa.q: What did Jasleen say that opened the way to be heard?
qa.a: Jasleen said "I probably don't know everything" and asked for two minutes without interruption, then to be told what was missed. That was calm and specific.

qa.q: How might Harbhajan have felt when Jasleen asked for two minutes?
qa.a: Harbhajan may have felt surprised, since Harbhajan blinked and sat back. The calm respect probably made it easy to listen without feeling attacked.

grounding: A young adult told "you don't know the world yet" calmly asks an elder uncle for a real hearing, as seen by a friend.
